answer: Node2vec does not rely on a single fixed start node per walk. Instead, for learning representations of all nodes, it runs r random walks of fixed length l starting from every node in the graph, and it repeats this over multiple passes, so each node appears as a walk start equally often and no node is systematically favored as a starting point. Because every node serves as a source of walks the same number of times, the start-node choice does not bias the resulting skip-gram training corpus toward any particular region of the graph. The walks are generated by a biased second-order random walk controlled by return parameter p and in-out parameter q, which interpolates between BFS-like (structural equivalence) and DFS-like (homophily) exploration. For efficiency, the transition probabilities for each (previous node, current node) pair are precomputed and stored as alias tables, so each step of a walk can be sampled in O(1) time after O(1)-per-edge preprocessing (alias setup costs roughly O(a^2 |V|) for second-order transitions, with a the average degree in the worst case, and can be reduced further by on-the-fly computation or approximations). Walks are then fed to the skip-gram model with negative sampling, which is trained with stochastic gradient descent, keeping the overall procedure scalable to large graphs.
